The members of the opposition party wanted to know that the government had promised to publish the objectives of any new trade agreement with the UK, but it was challenged that they would not publish them during the Brexit period. Hon. Chrystia Freeland (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs) introduced that Canada had an excellent assurance of its trade with the United States, which was our new NAFTA trade agreement that had negotiated, thanks to the unprecedented co-operation across this country. Anita Anand (Minister of Public Services and Procurement) explained that the Government of Canada had diversified supply chains internationally and built up and retool domestic industry so that Canada could have these supplies going forward. Mr. Alain Therrien suggested that during the pandemic, the government gave money to companies that did not pay a cent in tax because they used tax havens. The meeting was about the preparation for the upcoming meeting, where the team would present their work on the Aurora front-end and HTK acoustic models. Also, the team discussed how to deal with reverberation, which they thought could potentially be useful for noise estimation.

The team was two months away from completing the prototype of the TORRENT chip. The team needed to complete a rough draft of their proposal by Monday so that they could give it to Morgan for approval. They needed to run some tandem-style processing with their intermediate classifiers to build the intermediate categories. They also needed to figure out how to deal with pre-echo problems.

Grad F was focusing on the intermediate categories that he wanted to classify as a middle step. He would use the SRI recognizer since it was already set up for Switchboard and run some sort of tandem-style processing with his intermediate classifiers.

Grad F thought that he needed to come up with a complete set of intermediate features in intermediate categories to classify right away. He would start with a reasonable set of regular phonetic features and build a system that classifies these intermediate categories using multi-band techniques.

The SRI system had an improvement in word error rate training on TI-digits and testing on Meeting Recorder digits, but the near-mike performance worsened. Mean subtraction seemed to make the PZM signals louder after they had been re-segmented, suggesting that the finer-grained acoustic models could be more sensitive to the artifacts in re-sensitized audio. The professor was skeptical of this finding, pointing out that the improvement was due to channel normalization rather than noise reduction.

The professor explained that echo and reverberation were two concepts that had not been explored much in the literature. He thought that low-energy sections of speech were more likely to be affected by reverberation since they were lower energy. He also suggested doing mean normalization to get a better signal-to-noise ratio, but he did not think multiplying the signal by two would have any effect.

PhD C thought that the model was a little bit dependent on the absolute energy. The spectral subtraction that PhD C was doing seemed to have an effect on the signal, but not as much as the mean normalization.

Then they talked about the relationship between the governing bodies and the executive permanent staff and the governors, and the challenges they faced.

The first was the impact of the demographic dip of 18-year-olds, which is deeper and longer in Wales than it is elsewhere in the UK. The second was the increased pension costs and, actually, increased costs generally. The third was the current uncertainty as a result of the Augar review in England, and whether that might play into Wales, and also Brexit.

For example, Cardiff University have had a bond rather than borrowing, which they drew down as they were spending, so in the short term the reserves of Cardiff would appear as though they had significant cash balances, but all of those were restricted for investment in the estate over the next two or three years. Similarly, Swansea University had invested in their estates and that's largely funded by borrowings. The costs of those borrowings had to be met on an annual basis, so that's becoming an increasing proportion of the operating cash that universities have. Dr David Blaney confirmed that the estates strategies that institutions operate were overseen by either the full governing body or relevant sub-committees in respect of every institution, so there was proper governance oversight.

According to Dr David Blaney, the government was in a managed situation, where the institutions were alert to the challenges they were facing and were actually engaging those challenges properly, and they were seeing that at the moment. There was always the possibility of structural change within the sector, and that might be one of the solutions that institutions thought about, but it was not a policy position, and it's not always a good short-term response to crisis anyway, actually. They were keen to see what they could achieve with the sector in addressing these issues of what constitutes constructive challenge.

The government wanted to ensure that each university's estates strategy and its financing was prudent and had appropriate governing-body oversight in place. The machinery was in place to ensure proper governance oversight. The borrowing that the universities were undertaking was absolutely prudently assessed and was appropriate, but also, if the institutions were wanting to engage in anything other than relatively trivial borrowing, they had to get the government's consent.

The institutional risk review process was fundamentally designed to make sure that institutions were grappling with their problems before they become a crisis. 70/80 different factors and hundreds of questions would be asked twice a year to interrogate the performance of the institutions. The institutions were expected to look after the interest of the students.

It was suggested that more people should be involved in risk management, especially in the institutional risk review process, which has 70/80 different factors and hundreds of questions that are asked twice a year to interrogate the performance of the institutions and to make sure that they are seeing them managing the issues that they're facing.

Dr David Blaney thought it was fair to say that they were seeing an increased risk profile in the sector in Wales, and it was about the financial pressures that they had already discussed this morning. And that was why the efforts that the Minister had gone to to secure the Diamond settlement, and, indeed, other bits of money now and again, were so important. The institutions had been working very hard to try not to take cost out now that they really didn't have to take out, because they didn't want to reduce capacity, which they would struggle to recover again when the financial position improved.

Bethan Owen thought the key bit of that was maintaining the attractiveness of Welsh universities to students, because a large proportion were coming not from just Wales, but from England and internationally. That's a key part. Also, maintaining the institutions as attractive options for students and the research capacity was invested in would bring economic benefits.

Both the Diamond and Reid reviews called for QR funding to be maintained in real terms, but the allocation was exactly the same for 2019-20 as it had been for the past nine years. The reason the sum hasn't increased was because they had not had enough money to be able to increase it and still meet the obligations they had to other bits of the HE system. However, they would dearly love to increase the amount, for both Ian Diamond and Graeme Reid were very clear about the importance of being able to invest in their QR research funding, for a number of reasons. The capacity of the sector to respond to funding opportunities elsewhere in the UK and across the rest of the world was itself determined by the size and the strength of the research base, which was sustained by QR funding. And they knew that although the Welsh research base was extraordinarily productive, and really was punching above its weight in many ways, they could do so much more if they just had more scale.

Dr David Blaney said that not directly. It was sometimes more effective to have external experts making these points than us or the sector, so they relied on the expert assessment of people like Graeme Reid. But there was an assessment of the correlation between QR funding and capacity to generate funding from other sources, and there was a very close correlation. It had relied on expert assessments.

In 2017-18 and 2018-19, they were providing additional funding to WISERD Education, a research collaboration between a number of the Welsh universities, specifically looking at educational issues, to add value to the Welsh Government's existing evaluation of the progress of pioneer schools in developing the three-to-15 curriculum in Wales.

The Reid review had made recommendations to mitigate this impact. The assessment was that allocations would be able to help universities to transition away from EU funding. There had been an additional £6.6 million allocated for research very recently by the Government, which was put out specifically in line with some of the recommendations from Reid. However, that was not sustainable funding, and it was not enough, really, but it was a good and welcome start. Since it seemed possible at least, and possibly even likely, that any money retrieved from not having to invest in the EU would sit in London rather than necessarily being devolved to the devolved administrations, they understood fully the Welsh Government's position on that, and they didn't disagree with it. But either way, they needed a research base that's able to compete, and that's why the investment recommendations of Reid were so important.
